episode_title: Where Does a Leader’s Judgment Belong When AI Writes the First Draft? | AI for Executives

real_qa.q: What percentage of managers and above shifted their focus from creating outputs to managing AI-generated outputs according to the Wharton Human AI Research study reported by Fortune in October 2026?
real_qa.r: In 2026, a study from Wharton Human AI Research and GBK Collective, reported by Fortune on October 13, found that 72% of managers and above said their focus has shifted from creating outputs to managing AI-generated outputs. Among managers and directors, it was 63%, and among vice presidents and above, it was 82%.
real_qa.requete: Wharton AI 2026 managers managing AI outputs percentage

real_qa.q: What did the Wharton research paper 'Thinking Fast, Slow, and Artificial' find about confidence levels when AI provides wrong answers to reasoning puzzles?
real_qa.r: In the study by researchers at Wharton on reasoning puzzles, using AI raised people's confidence even after errors. Even when the AI had led them to the wrong answer, they felt more sure. Confidence went up whether the answer was right or wrong, which means feeling confident was a poor signal of being accurate when the AI was wrong.
real_qa.requete: Thinking Fast Slow Artificial Wharton AI confidence wrong answer

real_qa.q: How much did accuracy improve or decline in the Wharton study when participants consulted AI on reasoning puzzles compared to no AI?
real_qa.r: In study one, compared with no AI, accuracy rose 25 percentage points when the AI was right. Accuracy fell 15 points when the AI was wrong. So the AI did not just help or hurt a little, it pulled people strongly in which direction it pointed.
real_qa.requete: Wharton study AI accuracy 25 points 15 points wrong

real_qa.q: What is the recommended four-step practice for leaders to apply judgment when reviewing AI-generated drafts?
real_qa.r: Step one: before reading the AI draft, name the one part where an error could cost the most. Step two: check that part by hand against the source, not against the draft. Step three: read confidence as a feeling, not a fact—if the draft feels obviously right, that is the moment to check the costly part anyway. Step four: under time pressure, shrink the deck, don't skip it—check one part properly rather than abandon the check entirely.
real_qa.requete: leader judgment AI draft four steps check costly part

real_qa.q: Did time pressure or incentives remove the effect of raised confidence when AI provided wrong answers in the Wharton experiments?
real_qa.r: In study two, the researchers added time pressure. In study three, they added incentives and feedback with real reasons to get it right and information about how people were doing. Neither removed the effect. And people with higher trust in AI showed more of it.
real_qa.requete: Wharton study time pressure incentives AI confidence effect
